Package org.aristonis.diwan.database.eloquent.relations

Class MorphPivot

java.lang.Object
org.aristonis.diwan.database.eloquent.Model
org.aristonis.diwan.database.eloquent.relations.Pivot
org.aristonis.diwan.database.eloquent.relations.MorphPivot
public class MorphPivot extends Pivot
A row of a morph-to-many join table: a Pivot that also knows the type column and the type value of the relation that built it, such as taggables.taggable_type and Post. Laravel's MorphPivot.

A pivot with no key value writes by its two pivot keys and the type, so saving or deleting it never touches the row of another type that holds the same keys. A pivot with a key value writes by that key alone. The relation sets the type and the class; a pivot built any other way has neither, and then writes as a plain Pivot.

A write that sets the type column to a value other than the pivot's own type is refused, so a row never moves to another type, whatever a hook or listener does. Writing a row whose type column holds the pivot's own type is fine. The check applies only when a morph relation built the pivot; one built any other way has no morph type and is unchecked.

Not safe to share across threads, like every model.

    • beforeWrite

      protected final void beforeWrite()
      Refuses a write that sets the type column to a value other than this pivot's morph class. It runs after every saving, creating and updating hook and listener, just before the statement is built, so neither can change the type past it, and a subclass cannot skip it. A column named like the type column in another letter case is refused too, even with the right value, since the row would carry the column twice. A pivot not built by a morph relation, with no morph type set, is not checked.
      Overrides:
      beforeWrite in class Model
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if the type column holds another value; the message names the column, the value and the expected type

    • forceDelete

      public boolean forceDelete()
      Deletes the row for good, whether or not the model soft-deletes.

      Runs forceDeleting() first, then delete() (so deleting() and deleted() still run) with isForceDeleting() true, and forceDeleted() once the delete returned true. The flag is cleared even when a hook or the statement throws, so the next plain delete() soft-deletes again.

      Returns:
      true when deleted; false when a hook vetoed it or the model does not exist
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if the model does not soft-delete, or has no primary key
      QueryException - if the database refuses the statement

    • restore

      public boolean restore()
      Clears the deleted-at column and saves the model.

      Runs restoring() first; false from it stops the restore. The model is marked as existing, so a restore after a forceDelete() runs an UPDATE that touches no row and still returns true. A model whose column is already empty runs no statement. restored() runs after the save returned true.

      Returns:
      true when saved or already clean; false when a hook vetoed it
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if the model does not soft-delete
      QueryException - if the database refuses the statement

    • touchOwners

      public void touchOwners()
      Sets updated_at on the rows of each relation named in touches(), to now, a port of Laravel's touchOwners(). A save of a dirty model and a delete of an existing one call this on their own.

      Each relation sends one UPDATE built from this model's keys; no SELECT runs and no relation is loaded. The owner models already in memory keep their old updated_at. The touch goes on into an owner only when the relation is loaded on this model: a single loaded owner gets its saved() hook and then its own touches, each item of a loaded collection gets only its own touches. Within one call each model is walked once, and a cycle of loaded relations ends. A save() that a hook starts begins a new call. The recursion is as deep as the loaded chain, so a very deep loaded chain can overflow a small thread stack (Android). Owners of a class in a withoutTouching(Class, Runnable) scope are skipped.

      Throws:
      InvalidRelationException - if a name in touches() is not a relation of this model or names a relation type that does not support touches
      IllegalArgumentException - if a loaded relation value is not a model, a collection of models or null
      IllegalStateException - if the model class has no ModelQuery entry
      QueryException - if the database refuses an update

    • withoutTouching

      public static <V> V withoutTouching(Class<? extends Model> modelClass, Supplier<V> work)
      Runs work with owner touches of a class and its subclasses switched off on this thread, a port of Laravel's withoutTouchingOn([$class], ...); calls nest.

      Only the touch of an owner through a relation is skipped. Model.touch() and a model's own updated_at are not affected, and other threads, including one started inside the work, touch as usual. The scope ends when the work returns or throws.

      Type Parameters:
      V - the result type
      Parameters:
      modelClass - the owner class to leave untouched, never null
      work - the work, never null
      Returns:
      the value the work returns, may be null
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if an argument is null; no scope is opened then

      Parameters:

    • push

      public boolean push()
      Saves this model and then every model in its loaded relations, recursively, a port of Laravel's push().

      This model is saved first; when that save fails nothing else is visited. Then each loaded relation, in the order it was set, has its model or each model of its collection pushed the same way; a null relation is skipped. The first save that fails stops the walk and the call returns false. No transaction is opened, so the rows saved before the failure stay saved. Each save is the public Model.save(), so the saving and saved hooks and the owner touches run for every model.

      No foreign key is set: a new model put under a relation with setRelation is inserted with whatever key attributes it already has. A withDefault placeholder that a load put in the relations is inserted as well, as in Laravel. Within one call each model is saved once, so a cycle of loaded relations ends and a model reached by two paths is not saved twice (unlike Laravel, which saves it at each visit). The recursion is as deep as the loaded chain, so a very deep loaded chain can overflow a small thread stack (Android).

      Each save() inside the walk runs its own touch walk, so N dirty children that touch the same owner send N UPDATEs to that owner, as in Laravel.

      Returns:
      true when every model was saved or already clean, false when a hook vetoed a save
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if a loaded relation value is not a model, a collection of models or null
      IllegalStateException - if a model to save has no connection
      QueryException - if the database refuses a statement

    • toMap

      public Map<String,Object> toMap()
      Returns the model as a map of plain values: text, numbers, booleans, null, maps and lists, plus any value a cast or accessor returns that has no plain form.

      Appended keys follow the stored ones, each read through its accessor, and are subject to the visible and hidden lists like any other key. Loaded relations follow the appends, each under its name in snake case unless snakeRelationKeys() says otherwise, and filtered by the same visible and hidden lists: a model becomes its own map, a ModelCollection a list of maps, and a loaded null stays null. A relation key replaces an attribute of the same name.

      A model met again while it is already being serialised, as in a post whose author holds the same post, writes its attributes and appends only, so a cycle ends. The guard lets a model go once its own map is done, so an instance shared by several parents is written in full at each place it appears. With two-way relations loaded on many models, such as users holding their posts and each post holding its author, the output therefore grows with the product of the two sides — Laravel's behaviour too; drop one side with setHidden(List) or ModelRelations.withoutRelations() when that is too much.

      Returns:
      a new mutable map in attribute order, then append order, then relation order; never null
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if an appended key has no accessor with a getter; the message names the key
      InvalidCastException - if a cast cannot read or serialize a stored value, or an uncast timestamp column holds something that is not a moment

      public Map<String,Cast<?>> getCasts()
      Returns the resolved casts of this model: the class casts, then this instance's overlay from mergeCasts(Map), which wins for a key in both.

    • mergeCasts

      public Model mergeCasts(Map<String,?> casts)
      Adds casts to this instance only, on top of the class casts; a key already in the overlay or in casts() takes the new cast. Reads, writes, dirty checks and toMap() of this instance use it; the class casts and other instances are unchanged.

      A value is a Cast or a cast string as Casts.of(String) takes. Every value is resolved before anything changes, so a bad entry leaves the overlay as it was. Cached cast values are written back first, and those of the merged keys are dropped, so a key whose cast changed is read again through the new cast.

      Parameters:
      casts - the casts by attribute name, never null
      Returns:
      this model
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if casts or a key in it is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if a value is null or neither a cast nor a string
      InvalidCastException - if a cast string cannot be resolved

    • relations

      protected RelationMap<?> relations()
      Returns the relations the model declares, by name; none by default.

      Each entry builds one relation from a model, usually a reference to the model's typed relation method: 

      
 protected RelationMap<?> relations() {
     return RelationMap.of(Post.class).add("author", Post::author).add("comments", Post::comments);
 }

      The map names the relations that relation(name), eager loading and existence queries reach. It is read and checked once per model class, on first use, so it must not depend on instance state; a subclass inherits its parent's map. A bad map throws InvalidRelationException on that first use.

      Returns:
      the relation map, never null

    • touches

      protected Set<String> touches()
      Returns the names of the relations whose owners this model touches; none by default, a port of Laravel's $touches.

      Saving a dirty model, or deleting an existing one, sets the updated_at column of each named relation's rows to the current time, in the set's iteration order, so return a LinkedHashSet when the order matters: 

      
 protected Set<String> touches() {
     return new LinkedHashSet<>(Arrays.asList("post"));
 }

      Each name must be a key of relations() whose relation is a HasOne, HasMany or BelongsTo. The set is read and checked once per model class, on first use, so it must not depend on instance state; a bad name throws InvalidRelationException naming the class and the relation. A check that fails only because a related class has no ModelQuery entry yet is not cached and runs again on the next save. The bad entry is reported on first use, after the save that triggered it has written its row, so the exception reaches the caller with that row stored and the model left dirty.

      A touch is one raw UPDATE: it raises no model events, applies no casts and loads no model. The owner models already in memory keep their old updated_at value. The touch goes on into an owner only when that relation is already loaded on this model, where the owner's saved() hook runs and its own touches follow; unlike Laravel, an unloaded relation is never loaded for this. Like the relation map, this needs no reflection.

      save() runs no transaction: if a touch UPDATE fails, the child row is already written, the model stays dirty and the exception reaches the caller. Use saveOrFail() to make the save and its touches one transaction.

      Returns:
      the relation names, never null
